en: Sutta Nipāta 1.7 Vasalasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Now at that time, in the residence of the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja, a fire was blazing and an oblation had been prepared.
Then the Blessed One, wandering for alms from house to house in Sāvatthī, approached the residence of the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja.
The brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Stop right there, you shaveling!
Stop right there, you wretched ascetic!
Stop right there, you outcaste!”
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja:
“But do you know, brahmin, what an outcaste is, or the qualities that make one an outcaste?
“I do not indeed know, Master Gotama, what an outcaste is, or the qualities that make one an outcaste.”
“It would be well, venerable Gotama, if you would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand what an outcaste is, or the qualities that make one an outcaste.
“Then listen, brahmin, and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"The man who is prone to anger and resentment,
and who is malicious and slanderous;
One whose view is perverted and who is a deceiver—
know him as an outcaste,
whether he be once-born or twice-born.
He who harms living beings,
in whom there is no compassion for living beings—
he, you should know, is an outcaste.
He who kills and besieges villages and market towns is known as a suppressor.
One should know him as an outcast: whoever,
whether in the village or in the forest,
covets what belongs to others.
One who takes what is not given through theft—
one should know him as an outcaste (vasala).
He who, having indeed taken a loan...
Though being urged on, he flees;
"For you have no debt," they say—
know him to be an outcaste.
He who, seeing people traveling on the road desiring some trifle,
kills them and seizes that trifle—
One should know him as an outcaste:
that man who, for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of wealth, [acts thus].
One who, when questioned as a witness, speaks falsely—
one should know him as an outcaste (vasala).
He who [acts so] toward kinsmen or friends...
He is seen among his own wives;
whether through violence or through affection,
one should know him as an outcaste.
He who, though being wealthy, does not support his mother or father when they have grown old and lost their youth—
One should know him as an outcaste:
he who [neglects] his mother or father,
his brother, sister, or mother-in-law.
One who strikes or reviles with speech—
know him as an outcaste (vasala).
He who, when asked about the truth...
One who gives counsel that is not beneficial, and who deliberates with a concealed [intent],
one should know him as an outcaste.
He who, having committed an evil deed,
desires, "May no one know me," and whose actions are concealed—
One should know him as an outcaste:
he who, having gone to another's family,
eats pure food.
One who does not honor a visitor—
know him as an outcaste (vasala)—
whether he be a brahmin or a śramaṇa.
Or even another mendicant—
whosoever deceives by means of falsehood,
him one should know as an outcaste.
Whoever, when the time for a meal has arrived, offends a brahmin or a recluse with their speech and does not give [alms], [is reborn in hell].
One should know him as an outcaste:
he who here among the virtuous speaks falsely,
being shrouded by delusion.
One who seeks after trifles,
and who exalts himself— know him to be an outcaste.
But he despises others;
by that contemptuous pride,
one should know him as an outcaste.
One who is stingy and miserly,
one with evil desires, envious, and deceitful;
one who is shameless and lacks moral dread.
One should know him as an outcaste:
he who reviles the Buddha,
or else his disciple.
Whether he be a wanderer or a householder,
know him as an outcaste— whosoever,
while being unworthy, [claims to be otherwise].
He claims to be an Arahant;
he is a thief in this world together with its Brahmās—
this indeed is the lowest of outcasts.
These indeed are called outcasts,
as I have declared them.
One does not become an outcast by birth.
One does not become a brahmin by birth;
by one's deeds one becomes an outcaste,
and by one's deeds one becomes a brahmin.
Therefore, understand this also through this illustration:
Sopāka, the son of a caṇḍāla, was a scavenger.
Known as Mātaṅga,
he attained supreme fame—
fame that is very difficult to obtain.
Many kṣatriyas and brahmins came to attend upon him;
having ascended the celestial vehicle, they departed.
He [followed] that great path free from dust;
having removed lust for sensual pleasures,
he became one who goes to the Brahma-world.
Birth did not prevent him from being reborn in the Brahma-world;
he was born into a family of Vedic scholars.
The brahmins have mantras as their kinsmen;
yet they are frequently seen engaged in evil deeds.
They are censured in this very life,
and in the future there is a miserable rebirth;
even birth does not prevent this.
Regarding a miserable rebirth or censure:
One does not become an outcast by birth,
nor does one become a brahmin by birth.
“By action one becomes an outcaste;
by action one becomes a brahmin.
When this was said, the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
Thus ends the seventh discourse, the *Vasala Sutta*.
